--- title: "Explaining one prediction" description: "SHAP values split one prediction into a contribution from each input, starting from the model's average prediction and adding up to the prediction itself. On the survey they show which inputs lift a random forest's prediction at one station and pull it down at another." order: 3 categories: [interpretation] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## One prediction needs its own explanation [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd) and [partial effects](partial-effects.qmd) describe a model over every station at once. Often the question is about one station: a manager asks what makes the model predict many animals at a proposed monitoring site, or a reviewer wants to check a prediction that looks too high. The answer has to say which of that station's inputs moved its prediction, and by how much. This page splits one prediction into a share for each input. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## SHAP values share a prediction out among the inputs Imagine revealing a station's inputs to the model one at a time. Knowing none of them, its best guess is its average prediction over the training stations. Each input revealed moves the prediction up or down, and that move is credited to the input. The credit depends on the order: temperature revealed first may move the prediction more than temperature revealed after season, which carries some of the same information. So the moves are averaged over every order of revealing. An input's average move is its **SHAP value**. SHAP stands for SHapley Additive exPlanations: Shapley after the mathematician Lloyd Shapley, whose Shapley values share out a team's winnings fairly among its players, and additive because the values add up to the prediction, as shown below. ::: {.diagram} ![SHAP values in three steps: start from the average prediction, reveal the station's inputs in turn and credit each with the change it makes, averaged over every order, then add the contributions to reach the prediction.](img/shap-values.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Start from the average, no inputs known: three cells for inputs A, B and C, each showing a question mark, above a row of grey dots for the training stations' predictions with a blue line at their average. Reveal inputs in turn, each step shifts the guess: a step line that starts at a dashed average level, steps up when A is revealed, down a little when B is revealed and up again when C is revealed. Add the contributions, average plus contributions equals prediction: a bar for each input running from a dashed line at the average to a dashed line at the prediction, A and C blue and pointing right, B orange and pointing left. A note says that an input not yet revealed takes its values from the training stations, and the predictions are averaged."} ::: A model cannot leave an input blank, so an input not yet revealed takes each training station's value in turn, and the predictions are averaged. Because every order ends with all the inputs revealed, the SHAP values add up exactly: the average prediction plus every input's SHAP value equals the station's prediction. A positive value lifts the prediction above the average and a negative one pulls it below. ## Worked example A random forest of 500 trees, as in [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd), predicts abundance from six inputs and is fitted to the training sites of the same split by site. Two of the test stations are explained: one the forest predicts many animals for and one it predicts few for. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season") split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) forest_recipe <- recipe(reformulate(inputs, "abundance"), data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) forest_model <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |> set_mode("regression") forest <- workflow(forest_recipe, forest_model) |> fit(train) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import shap from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows].reset_index(drop=True) test = survey.iloc[test_rows].reset_index(drop=True) numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] inputs = numeric + categorical recipe = ColumnTransformer( [("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical)]) # max_features and min_samples_leaf match ranger's defaults model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123) forest = Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]).fit( train[inputs], train["abundance"]) ``` ::: ::: ### Shallow water lifts one station and warm water sinks another The high station is the test station whose prediction is above 90% of the others', and the low station the one whose prediction is above only 10%. With six inputs there are few enough orders to average over all of them, so the SHAP values are exact. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test$.pred <- predict(forest, test)$.pred # the test stations whose predictions sit nearest the 90th and 10th # percentiles: one predicted high, one predicted low nearest <- \(p) which.min(abs(test$.pred - quantile(test$.pred, p))) chosen <- test[c(nearest(0.9), nearest(0.1)), ] # SHAP values for the two stations; an input not yet revealed takes each # training station's value, and the predictions are averaged explained <- kernelshap(forest, X = chosen[inputs], bg_X = train[inputs], pred_fun = \(fitted, x) predict(fitted, x)$.pred, verbose = FALSE) # each station's inputs as recorded, beside their SHAP values shown <- \(row) map_chr(inputs, \(x) { value <- row[[x]] if (is.numeric(value)) format(round(value, 1), nsmall = 1) else as.character(value) }) tibble(Input = c(inputs, "Average prediction", "Prediction"), `High: value` = c(shown(chosen[1, ]), "", ""), `High: SHAP` = c(explained$S[1, ], explained$baseline, chosen$.pred[1]), `Low: value` = c(shown(chosen[2, ]), "", ""), `Low: SHAP` = c(explained$S[2, ], explained$baseline, chosen$.pred[2])) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Input |High: value | High: SHAP|Low: value | Low: SHAP| |:------------------|:-----------|----------:|:----------|---------:| |depth_m |44.9 | 0.95|55.5 | 0.02| |temperature_c |8.8 | 0.63|13.4 | -1.63| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 |2.1 | 0.80|1.0 | -0.42| |salinity_psu |33.3 | 0.58|33.4 | 0.06| |substrate |sand | -0.49|rock | -0.14| |season |spring | -0.05|summer | -0.45| |Average prediction | | 4.11| | 4.11| |Prediction | | 6.53| | 1.55|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} predicted = forest.predict(test[inputs]) # the test stations whose predictions sit nearest the 90th and 10th # percentiles: one predicted high, one predicted low nearest = lambda p: np.abs(predicted - np.quantile(predicted, p)).argmin() chosen = test.iloc[[nearest(0.9), nearest(0.1)]] # TreeExplainer computes exact SHAP values from the trees; an input not yet # revealed takes each training station's value explainer = shap.TreeExplainer( forest["model"], data=forest["recipe"].transform(train[inputs]), feature_perturbation="interventional") values = explainer.shap_values(forest["recipe"].transform(chosen[inputs])) # add the one-hot columns of substrate and season back into one value each columns = [next(x for x in inputs if name.split("__")[1].startswith(x)) for name in forest["recipe"].get_feature_names_out()] values = pd.DataFrame(values, columns=columns).T.groupby(level=0, sort=False).sum() rows = inputs + ["Average prediction", "Prediction"] shown = lambda row: [f"{v:.1f}" if isinstance(v, float) else v for v in row[inputs]] pd.DataFrame({ "Input": rows, "High: value": shown(chosen.iloc[0]) + ["", ""], "High: SHAP": list(values[0]) + [explainer.expected_value, predicted[nearest(0.9)]], "Low: value": shown(chosen.iloc[1]) + ["", ""], "Low: SHAP": list(values[1]) + [explainer.expected_value, predicted[nearest(0.1)]], }).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Input | High: value | High: SHAP | Low: value | Low: SHAP | |:-------------------|:--------------|-------------:|:-------------|------------:| | depth_m | 90.8 | -0.21 | 29.2 | 0.4 | | temperature_c | 10.0 | 0.45 | 15.4 | -1.72 | | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 1.8 | 1.38 | 0.9 | -0.18 | | salinity_psu | 33.5 | -0.13 | 33.5 | -0.11 | | substrate | mud | 0.61 | sand | -0.18 | | season | autumn | 0.11 | summer | -0.62 | | Average prediction | | 3.95 | | 3.95 | | Prediction | | 6.16 | | 1.54 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} waterfall <- function(row, title) { station <- chosen[row, ] steps <- tibble(input = inputs, shap = explained$S[row, ]) |> arrange(desc(abs(shap))) |> mutate(end = average + cumsum(shap), start = lag(end, default = average), label = paste0(names_of[input], " = ", shown(station)[match(input, inputs)], units_of[input]), label = fct_rev(fct_inorder(label)), direction = if_else(shap > 0, "lifts", "pulls down")) ggplot(steps, aes(y = label)) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(average, station$.pred), linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_segment(aes(x = start, xend = end, yend = label, colour = direction), linewidth = 7) + # each bar's SHAP value, in a column at the right geom_text(aes(x = 8.6, label = sprintf("%+.2f", shap), colour = direction), hjust = 1, size = 3.6) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(lifts = ml_palette[["blue"]], `pulls down` = ml_palette[["orange"]]), guide = "none") + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 8.6), breaks = seq(0, 8, 2)) + labs(title = title, x = "Predicted count (individuals)", y = NULL) } waterfall(1, glue::glue("High station: prediction {two(chosen$.pred[1])}")) / waterfall(2, glue::glue("Low station: prediction {two(chosen$.pred[2])}")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![SHAP values for the two test stations. Each bar starts where the one above it ends, from the forest's average prediction (left dashed line) to the station's prediction (right dashed line); blue bars lift the prediction and orange bars pull it down, by the SHAP value printed on the right. Each input is labelled with its value at the station.](explaining-one-prediction_files/figure-html/fig-waterfall-1.png){#fig-waterfall fig-alt='Two panels of horizontal bars, one bar per input, sharing a horizontal axis of predicted count. Each bar starts where the one above ends. Top, the high station: from the average prediction of 4.11 the bars step depth up 0.95, chlorophyll up 0.80, temperature up 0.63, salinity up 0.58, substrate down 0.49, season down 0.05, ending at the prediction of 6.53. Bottom, the low station: from the same average they step temperature down 1.63, season down 0.45, chlorophyll down 0.42, substrate down 0.14, salinity up 0.06, depth up 0.02, ending at the prediction of 1.55.' width=1600} ::: ::: The forest's average prediction over the training stations is 4.11 individuals. At the high station, 44.9 m deep, depth lifts the prediction by 0.95, and chlorophyll, temperature and salinity add 2.01 between them; its sand substrate pulls it down by 0.49, ending at 6.53. The low station is in water of 13.4 °C in summer, and temperature alone pulls its prediction down by 1.63. Season, which carries some of the same information, takes off another 0.45, and chlorophyll 0.42, ending at 1.55. Each station's bars add up exactly from the average to its prediction. The same input can play different parts at different stations. Temperature lifts one prediction and sinks the other, because the high station's water, at 8.8 °C, lies on the hump in [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd), and the low station's lies beyond its warm side. ## A SHAP value explains the prediction, not whether it is right Chlorophyll lifts the high station's prediction by 0.80 and pulls the low station's down by 0.42, yet in [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd) shuffling it barely changed the forest's test error. The two measure different things. A SHAP value says what a prediction rests on, whether or not the prediction is accurate; permutation importance says how much the accuracy rests on an input. The forest uses chlorophyll in its predictions, but its test error hardly depends on it. Like the other tools in this section, SHAP values describe the model, not the species. [Interpretable models and surrogates](interpretable-models.qmd) turns to models whose parts can be read directly. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A **SHAP value** is one input's share of one prediction: the change it makes when revealed, averaged over every order of revealing the inputs. - The average prediction plus every input's SHAP value equals the prediction, so the values say exactly where a prediction comes from. - An input not yet revealed takes the training stations' values in turn, and the predictions are averaged; this works for any model. - On the survey, depth lifted the forest's prediction at a shallow station, and warm summer water pulled it down at another. - A SHAP value explains a prediction, not whether it is right; permutation importance measures what the accuracy depends on. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Explain the test station with the highest prediction. Which input lifts it most, and is its value common in the survey? 2. Explain the high station again, with only 50 training stations to fill in the inputs not yet revealed. How much do its SHAP values change?
